content: The most frequently reported adverse events in clinical studies included headache (22%), fatigue or asthenia (16%), and abdominal pain (10%). A case of thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 359 x 10³/μL) was observed on Day 31 in a nine-year-old boy treated with a combination of ombitasvir (OBV), paritaprevir (PTV), ritonavir, and other drugs. This event was attributed to a concurrent respiratory illness. In the sofosbuvir (SOF) and velpatasvir (VEL) treatment group, two adverse events were reported: one involving auditory hallucinations in a six-year-old girl. Among adolescents aged 12–18 years, 50% experienced at least one adverse event, with the most common being headache (22%), fatigue or asthenia (14%), and nausea (9%). Serious adverse events were reported in eight adolescents, including two cases of serious pneumonia in patients treated with SOF and ledipasvir (LDV). Other serious adverse events unrelated to the drugs included a fractured finger and dyspepsia requiring intravenous hydration in the elbasvir (EBR) and grazoprevir (GZR) group, a broken leg in the SOF + LDV group, and hypotension in one adolescent treated with SOF + VEL + voxilaprevir (VOX). A meta-analysis of adverse events in children aged 3–5 years with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection treated with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) revealed that headache, fatigue, and nausea were the most common side effects. Similar findings were observed in children aged 6–11 years and adolescents aged 12–18 years. The quality of life in children with HCV infection was significantly impaired, affecting physical, psychosocial, and cognitive functioning, and increasing caregiver stress and family strain. Studies using standardized questionnaires demonstrated that children with HCV had lower scores in physical functioning, general health, and emotional well-being compared to healthy peers. Treatment with DAAs, such as SOF + LDV, SOF + VEL, and glecaprevir (GLC) + pibrentasvir (PIB), was highly effective in achieving sustained virologic response (SVR12) across all pediatric age groups. SVR12 rates were 95% for children aged 3–5 years, 99% for those aged 6–11 years, and 99% for adolescents aged 12–18 years. The efficacy of these regimens was comparable to that observed in adults. Adverse events were generally mild, and treatment discontinuation was rare. The most common adverse events included headache, fatigue, and nausea, with no significant differences between treatment regimens or age groups. Quality of life improved significantly after achieving SVR12, particularly in emotional and school functioning domains. Caregivers also reported reduced stress and improved perceptions of their children’s health. Studies suggest that initiating treatment during childhood is cost-effective compared to deferring treatment until adulthood, especially with the use of pangenotypic regimens. The strength of evidence for DAA efficacy varied by age group and regimen. For children aged 3–5 years, evidence was moderate for SOF + LDV and very low for other regimens due to limited data. For children aged 6–11 years, evidence was moderate to high for SOF + DCV, SOF + LDV, and GLC + PIB, while evidence for other regimens was very low. Among adolescents aged 12–18 years, evidence was high for SOF + DCV and moderate for other regimens. In conclusion, treating children and adolescents with chronic HCV infection using DAAs is highly effective and safe, with SVR12 rates comparable to those in adults. The treatment improves quality of life and reduces the stigma associated with HCV infection. However, further research is needed to address gaps in data, particularly for younger children and those with comorbidities or coinfections.
